title: Dividing Whole Numbers (up to 1000 ÷ 2-digit)
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Number
summary: Estimate and divide whole numbers up to 1000 by 1-digit and 2-digit numbers using short division, chunking and long division, and decide what to do with remainders.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Estimate the answer to a division before you calculate it, and use the estimate to check (6Ni.05).
Divide whole numbers up to 1000 by a 1-digit number (for example 935 ÷ 4) or a 2-digit number (for example 989 ÷ 23), and deal with remainders sensibly in word problems (6Ni.05).

blocks.text: Division means sharing equally or grouping. It is the **inverse** (opposite) of multiplication: if 142 × 6 = 852, then 852 ÷ 6 = 142. On this page you will learn to estimate, to use **short division** ("bus stop"), **chunking** and **long division**, and to decide what to do with a **remainder** in a real problem.
Key words

items: dividend
المقسوم — the number being divided (852 in 852 ÷ 6)
divisor
المقسوم عليه — the number you divide by (6 in 852 ÷ 6)
quotient
خارج القسمة — the answer (142)
remainder
الباقي — what is left over when the division is not exact; written r, e.g. 935 ÷ 4 = 233 r 3
divisible by
يقبل القسمة على — divides exactly, with no remainder
multiple
مضاعف — the result of multiplying a number by a whole number (24, 48, 72 … are multiples of 24)
inverse
العملية العكسية — multiplication undoes division and division undoes multiplication
estimate
تقدير — a quick, close answer using friendly numbers

blocks.text: Remember: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient remainder, and the **check** is quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
1. Estimate first: use friendly numbers
For division do not just round to the nearest hundred. Change the dividend to a nearby number that **divides easily** because you know a multiplication fact. These are called **compatible numbers**.
You can also find **which two tens** the answer lies between: for 768 ÷ 24, 24 × 30 = 720 and 24 × 40 = 960, so the answer is between 30 and 40 (and close to 30).
2. Short division (÷ a 1-digit number)

items: Write the dividend inside the "bus stop" and the divisor outside on the left.
Start at the **left** (the biggest place value). How many 6s in 8? **1**, remainder 2. Write 1 on top.
Carry the remainder 2 to the next digit: it makes **25**. How many 6s in 25? **4**, remainder 1.
Carry the 1: it makes **12**. How many 6s in 12? **2**, remainder 0.
Answer 142. Check: 142 × 6 = 852 ✓ (and 142 is close to the estimate 140).

blocks.text: In 935 ÷ 4: 9 ÷ 4 = 2 r 1 → 13 ÷ 4 = 3 r 1 → 15 ÷ 4 = 3 r 3. Nothing is left to carry into, so the answer is **233 r 3**. Check: 233 × 4 + 3 = 932 + 3 = 935 ✓

**Two special cases.** (1) If the first digit is smaller than the divisor, look at the first two digits: 315 ÷ 7 → 3 ÷ 7 = 0, so work out 31 ÷ 7 = 4 r 3, then 35 ÷ 7 = 5. Answer 45. (2) If a step gives 0, you **must write the 0** in the answer: 624 ÷ 6 → 6 ÷ 6 = 1, 2 ÷ 6 = **0** r 2, 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Answer **104**, not 14.
3. Dividing by a 2-digit number: chunking

Chunking means taking away big, easy **chunks** (multiples of the divisor) until nothing (or only a remainder) is left. Then add up how many lots you took. Start by writing a few easy multiples of the divisor: 1×, 2×, 5×, 10×, 20×.

blocks.text: Bigger chunks = fewer steps. Using 30 × 24 = 720 straight away: 768 − 720 = 48 = 2 × 24, so the answer is 30 + 2 = 32.
4. Long division (÷ a 2-digit number)
Long division is the written method for chunking. Each step has the same four parts: **Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down** (remember "**D**oes **M**y **S**ister **B**ake?").

items: 989 ÷ 23. 23 does not go into 9, so use 98. **Divide:** 23 × 4 = 92 and 23 × 5 = 115 (too big), so write 4 above the 8.
**Bring down** the next digit 9 to make 69.
**Divide:** 23 × 3 = 69, so write 3 above the 9. Multiply and subtract: 69 − 69 = 0.
No digits left. Answer **43**, remainder 0. Check: 43 × 23 = 989 ✓ and 43 is close to the estimate 40.

blocks.text: When the division is not exact, the last subtraction leaves a remainder. The remainder must always be **smaller than the divisor** — if it is not, your quotient digit is too small.

blocks.text: **Short division by a 2-digit number** works too if you list multiples first. For 864 ÷ 16: list 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96. 86 ÷ 16 = 5 r 6 (5 × 16 = 80), then 64 ÷ 16 = 4. Answer **54**.

blocks.title: بالعربي: خطوات القسمة المطولة
blocks.text: كل خطوة فيها 4 حاجات: اقسم ← اضرب ← اطرح ← نزّل الرقم اللي بعده. ولو القسمة على رقمين، اكتب الأول جدول صغير لمضاعفات المقسوم عليه (×1، ×2، ×5، ×10). وافتكر: الباقي لازم يكون أصغر من المقسوم عليه، ولو خطوة طلعت صفر لازم تكتب الصفر في الناتج (624 ÷ 6 = 104 مش 14).
5. Remainders in real life
In a word problem you must decide what the remainder **means**. Read the question again before you write the answer.

rows: 460 students, 52 seats on each bus. How many buses?
Mona has 500 pounds. A book costs 35 pounds. How many books can she buy?
**14 books** (10 pounds is not enough for another)
900 cups packed in boxes of 24. How many cups are left over?

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** (1 mark) — Ring the best estimate for 618 ÷ 8.   7   60   80   700
640 is close to 618 and 64 ÷ 8 = 8, so 640 ÷ 8 = 80. **Answer: 80.** (Exact: 77 r 2.) Common mistake: 700 — that is the dividend rounded, not the quotient.
**Worked example 2** (1 mark) — Calculate 624 ÷ 6.
6 ÷ 6 = 1. 2 ÷ 6 = 0 remainder 2 → write **0**, carry 2. 24 ÷ 6 = 4. **Answer: 104.** Check: 104 × 6 = 624 ✓. Common mistake: writing 14. Estimate 600 ÷ 6 = 100 shows that 14 is far too small.
**Worked example 3** (2 marks) — Calculate 816 ÷ 34. Show your working.

items: Estimate: 800 ÷ 40 = 20 (or 816 is about 850 = 25 × 34), so the answer is between 20 and 25.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** (1 mark) — 460 students go on a school trip. Each bus has 52 seats. How many buses are needed?

460 ÷ 52: 52 × 8 = 416, 52 × 9 = 468 (too big). 460 − 416 = 44, so 460 ÷ 52 = 8 r 44. The 44 students still need a bus, so round **up**. **Answer: 9 buses.** Common mistake: writing "8 r 44" or "8" — a remainder is never the final answer to a "how many buses/boxes are needed" question.
**Worked example 5** (1 mark) — When a number is divided by 15 the answer is 42 remainder 7. What is the number?
Use the inverse: number = quotient × divisor + remainder = 42 × 15 + 7 = 630 + 7 = **637**. Check: 637 ÷ 15 → 15 × 42 = 630, remainder 7 ✓
**Worked example 6** (2 marks) — 932 ÷ 7. Give your answer with a remainder, then explain how to check it.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Missing a **0** in the quotient (624 ÷ 6 = 104, not 14; 972 ÷ 9 = 108, not 18).
Starting from the right as in multiplication — division starts from the **left**.
A remainder bigger than (or equal to) the divisor — your quotient digit was too small.
Forgetting to carry the remainder to the next digit in short division.
Writing "8 r 44 buses" — in context, round up or down and give a whole-number answer with units.
Mixing up dividend and divisor: 52 ÷ 460 is not the same as 460 ÷ 52.
Not checking with the inverse: quotient × divisor + remainder should give the dividend.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Calculate 816 ÷ 34" with a working space — show chunks or long division; working can earn a method mark.
"Ring the best estimate" — choose friendly numbers from a known fact.
Word problems with remainders: "How many boxes are needed?" (round up), "How many can she buy?" (round down), "How many are left over?" (the remainder).
Missing digits in a written division — use the inverse and work digit by digit.
"A number is divided by … the answer is … remainder …. Find the number." — multiply, then add the remainder.
"Tick the division that has a remainder" — check quickly with tests of divisibility (see the Factors page).
On Paper 2 (calculator) a remainder shows as a decimal: 460 ÷ 52 = 8.846… — you still have to decide whether to round up or down.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Division practice
blocks.intro: Paper 1 style: no calculator. Estimate first, work on paper, then type the answer. Think about what the remainder means in word problems.

questions.q: Which is the best estimate for 917 ÷ 3?
(a) What is the whole-number answer (the quotient)?
350 guests are coming to a wedding. Each table seats 12 guests. How many tables are needed?
questions.e: 350 ÷ 12: 12 × 29 = 348, remainder 2. The 2 extra guests need a table, so round up: 30 tables.

questions.q: A cinema ticket costs 45 pounds. Youssef has 800 pounds. What is the greatest number of tickets he can buy?
questions.e: 800 ÷ 45: 45 × 17 = 765, 45 × 18 = 810 (too much). 17 r 35. 35 pounds is not enough for another ticket, so round down: 17 tickets.

questions.q: When a number is divided by 13, the answer is 56 remainder 9. What is the number?
Which of these divisions has a remainder?
questions.e: 945 ÷ 5 = 189, 846 ÷ 9 = 94, 912 ÷ 8 = 114 are exact. 735 is odd, so it cannot be divided exactly by 6 (6 is even): 735 ÷ 6 = 122 r 3.

questions.q: Hana works out 588 ÷ 14 = 42. Which calculation checks her answer?
questions.e: Multiplication is the inverse of division: 42 × 14 = 588 ✓

questions.q: Ahmed says that 832 ÷ 8 = 14. Explain his mistake and give the correct answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explains that 3 ÷ 8 = 0 so a 0 must be written in the tens place (oe, e.g. "he left out the zero", or uses an estimate: 800 ÷ 8 = 100 so 14 is too small). 1 mark: correct answer 104.
questions.e: 8 ÷ 8 = 1; 3 ÷ 8 = 0 r 3 (write 0); 32 ÷ 8 = 4. Answer 104. Ahmed left out the 0. Estimate check: 800 ÷ 8 = 100, so 14 cannot be right.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Estimate with **friendly numbers** from a known fact (618 ÷ 8 ≈ 640 ÷ 8 = 80).
Short division starts from the **left**; carry each remainder to the next digit; write any **0** in the answer.
For a 2-digit divisor, list easy multiples (×1, ×2, ×5, ×10, ×20) and chunk, or use long division: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down.
The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
In word problems decide: round **up**, round **down**, or the remainder **is** the answer.
Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
